chapter.title: Know who's walking with you

cards.body: Picture leading a walk to a lighthouse. If the 4 people with you grew up in this town, you skip the bit about where the harbour is. If they arrived this morning, that bit is the whole walk. **The route changes with who is walking it.** Same destination, different steps, because the steps are for them, not for you.
cards.simpler: Imagine you are leading a walk to a lighthouse with 4 people. If they grew up in this town, you skip the part about where the harbour is. If they arrived this morning, that part is the whole walk. **The route changes with who is walking it.** Same place at the end, different steps along the way, because the steps are for them, not for you.

cards.prompt: You're giving a 3-minute talk on why your cafe should switch to oat milk. The listeners are the 3 baristas who make 200 coffees a day. Which part do you cut?

options.text: The 40 seconds explaining what a flat white is
The 40 seconds on how oat milk foams differently
The one sentence saying what you're asking them to do

whyNot.b: That's the part they don't know yet, not the part they already know: foaming is new to them and it's the thing that affects their day.
whyNot.c: That's your destination from chapter 1, not background: the one sentence always stays.

cards.reteach: Cut what the listeners already know, keep what they don't. Baristas know what a flat white is. They don't know how oat milk behaves, and that's what they'll care about, so it stays.

cards.title: Three lines about them
cards.body:
Before you plan a single step, write 3 lines about the people listening. Line 1: what they already know about your topic. Line 2: what they care about, meaning what would make their week better or worse. Line 3: what they'll be thinking when you stand up, like *hungry*, *sceptical* or *I've heard this pitch before*.

**Anything they already know gets cut.** Not shortened. Cut. A 3-minute talk has room for about 400 words, and every word spent telling people something they know is a word not spent getting them to the destination.
cards.simpler:
Before you plan anything, write 3 lines about the people who will listen. Line 1: what they already know about your topic. Line 2: what they care about, meaning what would make their week better or worse. Line 3: what they will be thinking when you stand up, like *hungry*, *sceptical* or *I've heard this before*.

**Anything they already know gets cut.** Not made shorter. Cut. A 3-minute talk holds about 400 words. Every word spent on what they already know is a word lost.

cards.title: The same talk, twice
cards.body:
Dev had to pitch a shared team calendar. To the 5 engineers, his 3 lines read: *know we miss meetings, care about fewer interruptions, thinking 'another tool?'* To the office manager, Rita, they read: *knows nothing about our tools, cares about room bookings, thinking 'will this make my job harder?'*

For the engineers he cut the whole explanation of what a shared calendar does. For Rita he cut everything about notifications and kept 30 seconds on room bookings. Same destination, 2 different routes. Rita said yes in the meeting. The engineers asked for a link.
cards.simpler:
Dev had to pitch a shared team calendar. For the 5 engineers, his 3 lines read: *know we miss meetings, care about fewer interruptions, thinking 'another tool?'* For Rita, the office manager, they read: *knows nothing about our tools, cares about room bookings, thinking 'will this make my job harder?'*

For the engineers he cut the whole explanation of what a shared calendar does. For Rita he cut everything about notifications and kept 30 seconds on room bookings. Same goal, 2 different routes. Rita said yes in the meeting. The engineers asked for a link.

cards.prompt: Your talk is 'we should run the Saturday 5k in the park, not on the road'. Your listeners are 6 people who have done the road route 20 times. Which 3 lines fit them?

options.text: Know nothing about the route, care about safety, thinking 'what's a 5k?'
Know the road route by heart, care about not getting bored, thinking 'why change what works?'
Know the park well, care about parking, thinking 'I'm late'

whyNot.a: That's a group of beginners, not people who've run it 20 times: they know the route, so you'd be writing lines for the wrong walkers.
whyNot.c: That's guessing at details you don't have, not using what you know: nothing says they know the park or drive there. Start from what the scenario tells you.

cards.reteach: The 3 lines come from what you actually know about the listeners. These 6 have run the road 20 times, so line 1 is 'they know the route'. People who repeat something 20 times often fear change and boredom, so lines 2 and 3 follow from that.

cards.title: What they care about decides what stays
cards.body:
Line 2 does the real work. **What they care about is the only reason they'll follow you.** Dev's engineers cared about interruptions, so his talk became 'this cuts interruptions'. Rita cared about rooms, so hers became 'this stops double bookings'. Same tool, 2 different sentences.

This isn't bending the truth. It's choosing which true thing to say first. You have 3 minutes. Spend them on the part of your point that touches their week, and leave the rest for the questions afterwards.

If you can't fill line 2, you're not ready to plan the route. Ask someone who'll be in the room. One text message is enough.

cards.body: Sam gave a talk about a new filing system to 8 colleagues who had used the old one for 6 years. He opened with 2 minutes on how filing works. By the time he reached the new part, people were checking phones. You can spot this one yourself: read your draft and mark every sentence your listeners could have said to you. If more than 1 or 2 are marked, you've written it for strangers.
cards.simpler: Sam gave a talk about a new filing system to 8 colleagues. They had used the old system for 6 years. He opened with 2 minutes on how filing works. By the time he reached the new part, people were checking their phones. You can catch this yourself. Read your draft and mark every sentence your listeners could have said to you. If more than 1 or 2 are marked, you have written it for strangers.

cards.prompt: You've written your 3 lines and your draft. A friend asks: 'how do you decide what to cut?' What do you tell them?

options.text: Cut whatever makes the talk longer than 3 minutes, starting from the end
Cut whatever the listeners already know, and keep what touches what they care about
Cut whatever you feel least confident saying out loud

whyNot.a: That's trimming by the clock, not by the listener: you could cut the one thing they needed and keep 40 seconds they already knew.
whyNot.c: That's about your nerves, not their needs: chapter 6 covers nerves. Here the listener decides, not your comfort.

cards.reteach: Your 3 lines tell you two things: what they know and what they care about. Cut the first, build around the second. Length sorts itself out once you stop telling people what they already know.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Write 3 lines about your listeners before you plan: what they know, what they care about, what they're thinking. **Cut anything they already know**, and build the talk around what they care about.
cards.simpler: Before you plan, write 3 lines about your listeners: what they know, what they care about, and what they are thinking. Think of it like packing for a trip. You only bring what the people with you will need. **Cut anything they already know**, and build the whole talk around what they care about. Everything else can wait for the questions afterwards.

cards.body: Take the one sentence from chapter 1. Write 3 lines about the people you'd most likely say it to. Then text one of them a single question: 'what do you already know about this?'
cards.simpler: Take the one sentence you wrote in chapter 1. Now write 3 lines about the people you would most likely say it to: what they know, what they care about, what they will be thinking. Then text one of them a single question: 'what do you already know about this?' Their answer tells you where the walk really starts. **One text message is enough** to find out.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now describe your audience in 3 lines and cut any part of your talk they don't need.
